questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: Which three elements make up the ACC/AHA 2017 definition of heart failure?
opts: A single arrhythmia; lung disease; increased urine output
Isolated chest pain; a normal heart; preserved filling and ejection
A complex clinical syndrome; a structural or functional cardiac disorder; impaired ventricular filling or ejection
Fever and leucocytosis; valve calcification; normal output
questions.exp: The definition bullets read complex clinical syndrome, any structural/functional cardiac disorder and impaired ability of the ventricle to fill with or eject blood. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: Which examples and expansions are printed directly beneath the definition?
opts: Structural pericarditis and functional edema; both abbreviations are left unexpanded
Structural CAD and functional COPD; AHA is American Hospital Association
Structural LVH and functional arrhythmia such as AF; ACC is expanded as American College of Clinical Cardiology and AHA as American Heart Association
Structural MR and functional anemia; ACC is American College of Cardiology only
questions.exp: The page gives structural LVH, functional arrhythmia/atrial fibrillation and expands ACC and AHA; the ACC expansion 'American College of Clinical Cardiology' is preserved as printed. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: Match each heart-failure type to its printed EF definition — 1) HFrEF 2) HFpEF/HFNEF 3) HFmrEF 4) ADHF … A) Acute decompensated heart failure B) Preserved/normal EF ≥50% C) Reduced EF <40% D) Mid-range EF 40–50%
questions.exp: The four lines define HFrEF <40%, HFpEF/HFNEF ≥50%, HFmrEF 40–50% and ADHF as acute decompensated heart failure. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: The first-line symptoms in the NYHA section are angina, dyspnea and palpitation; ______ is explicitly not part of NYHA.
questions.exp: The two bullets read first-line symptoms angina, dyspnea, palpitation and 'Syncope is not a part of NYHA'. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: Match each NYHA class to its printed criterion — 1) Class I 2) Class II 3) Class III 4) Class IV … A) Symptoms with less than ordinary activity B) Symptoms with more than ordinary activity C) Symptoms at rest D) Symptoms with ordinary physical activity
questions.exp: Rows I–IV print symptoms with more than ordinary activity, ordinary physical activity, less than ordinary activity and at rest, respectively. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: Match each NYHA class to the mortality entry as drawn — 1) Class I 2) Class II–III 3) Class IV … A) LV-failure symptoms B) Negligible mortality C) Sudden cardiac death
questions.exp: The mortality column places negligible mortality against class I, sudden cardiac death across classes II–III and LV-failure symptoms against class IV. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: A patient develops breathlessness only while climbing his usual flight of stairs, with no symptoms at rest. According to the printed NYHA row, which class is this?
opts: Class I — symptoms with more than ordinary activity
Class II — symptoms with ordinary physical activity
Class III — symptoms with less than ordinary activity
questions.exp: Ordinary physical activity maps to class II in the NYHA table. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the p318 definitions.
opts: True — HFpEF/HFNEF is printed with preserved/normal EF ≥50%
False — syncope is one of the three first-line NYHA symptoms
True — HFrEF is printed with EF >70%
False — ADHF means chronic stable heart failure
questions.exp: The page prints HFpEF/HFNEF ≥50%, HFrEF <40%, syncope outside NYHA and ADHF as acute decompensated heart failure. (Book p318)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
questions.q: Match each heart-failure stage to its defining characteristic — 1) A 2) B 3) C 4) D … A) Structural disease but no symptoms B) Risk factors only, no symptoms or structural disease C) Refractory, no response to medical therapy D) Most common; symptomatic now or previously
questions.exp: Stage A has risk factors only, B structural disease without symptoms, C is most common and symptomatic (prior/present), and D is refractory with no response to any medical therapy. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features

opts: Hypertension, atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus and obstructive sleep apnea
MI, LVH, cardiac remodelling and AF
questions.exp: The stage-A bullets list HTN, atherosclerosis, DM and OSA. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
questions.q: Stage B has no symptoms but structural heart disease, exemplified by an HTN patient with LVH and a previous MI with ______.
questions.exp: The two stage-B examples are HTN patient → LVH and previous MI → cardiac remodelling. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
questions.q: What is printed as the most common presentation of heart failure?
questions.exp: The note lists HFrEF, NYHA 2/3 and stage C as the most common presentation. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
questions.q: Match the two named systolic-failure mechanisms to their printed consequences — 1) Fatigue 2) Decreased cardiac output 3) Cool extremities and cyanosis 4) Pulsus alternans and narrow pulse pressure … A) Left-sided HF symptoms B) Cachexia from TNF-α C) Peripheral hypoperfusion D) Listed as low-output signs
questions.exp: Fatigue leads to cachexia with TNF-α as cause; decreased CO indicates left-sided HF symptoms; cool extremities/cyanosis reflect hypoperfusion; pulsus alternans and narrow pulse pressure are the final low-output signs. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
questions.q: Which complete ten-item systolic-failure list is printed on page 319?
opts: Fatigue, decreased urine output, cool extremities, cyanosis, altered mentation, S3, cardiomegaly, displaced apex, pulsus alternans and narrow pulse pressure
Bendopnea, trepopnea, platypnea, cough, wheeze, obesity, AF, CKD, anemia and diabetes
Dyspnea, crackles, pleural effusion, orthopnea, PND, ascites, edema, JVP, hepatomegaly and tachycardia
Angina, syncope, fever, murmur, cannon waves, A2, P2, S4, OS and click
questions.exp: The low-output list numbers fatigue with cachexia/TNF-α, decreased urine output, cool extremities, cyanosis, altered mentation, S3, cardiomegaly (dilated LV), displaced apex, pulsus alternans and narrow pulse pressure. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
questions.q: A patient with HFrEF has altered mentation, cold cyanotic extremities, oliguria and a narrow pulse pressure. Which category does the page assign to these findings?
opts: Systolic or LV forward-failure symptoms from decreased cardiac output
questions.exp: The HFrEF section labels these as systolic-failure/LV-forward symptoms due to decreased cardiac output and left-sided HF. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one item belongs to the later diastolic/right-failure list rather than the p319 low-output ten.
questions.exp: Ascites appears under right-heart failure on p321; altered mentation, cardiomegaly and pulsus alternans are in the systolic low-output ten. (Book p319)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: Which two upstream abnormalities converge on raised LVEDP in the diastolic-failure diagram?
opts: Concentric LVH with reduced cavity size/volume and systolic failure with insufficient dilation plus increased ESV
Wide pulse pressure and aortic regurgitation
questions.exp: The two arms read concentric LVH → cavity size/volume ↓ and systolic failure → insufficient dilation → ESV ↑, both converging on ↑LVEDP. (Book p320)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: Match the next three steps of the pressure chain — 1) Raised LVEDP 2) Raised LAP 3) Raised PCVP … A) Pulmonary exudation B) Raised left atrial pressure C) Raised pulmonary capillary venous pressure
questions.exp: The vertical chain runs ↑LVEDP → ↑LAP → ↑PCVP → pulmonary exudation. (Book p320)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: Which three consequences of pulmonary exudation are listed?
opts: Dyspnea (the predominant HF symptom), crackles in acute presentation and mostly right-sided pleural effusion with a preference to lie on the right side
questions.exp: The final three bullets are dyspnea (predominant symptom in HF), crackles (acute presentation) and pleural effusion mostly right-sided with right-side lying preference. (Book p320)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: How do the printed timings distinguish orthopnea from PND?
opts: Orthopnea occurs after 2–3 hours; PND is immediate
Both occur only after standing 30 seconds
Orthopnea is after 5 years and PND after 3 years
Orthopnea is immediate after lying down; PND occurs after 2–3 hours of lying down
questions.exp: The two lines print orthopnea immediately after lying down and PND after 2–3 hours. (Book p320)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: The PND mechanism begins when the patient lies supine and increased fluid shifts from the ______ to the intravascular compartment.
questions.exp: The flowchart reads increased fluid shift from interstitial to intravascular compartment. (Book p320)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: Which chain follows the fluid shift in PND?
opts: Right atrium → pulmonary circulation → not accommodated by a patient in heart failure → symptomatic air hunger
Left atrium → systemic circulation → renal excretion → relief
questions.exp: The lower arrows read RA → pulmonary circulation → not accommodated by patient in heart failure → patient becomes symptomatic (air hunger). (Book p320)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: A patient becomes breathless the moment he reclines but has no delayed waking episodes. Which printed presentation is this?
questions.exp: Orthopnea is dyspnea immediately after lying down, while PND occurs 2–3 hours later. (Book p320)

questions.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one step is not in the p320 PND mechanism.
opts: The failing patient cannot accommodate the shift and develops air hunger
Fluid enters the right atrium and pulmonary circulation
Decreased fluid shift from intravascular to interstitial compartment
questions.exp: The page prints an increased interstitial-to-intravascular shift, not the reverse direction. (Book p320)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: The most common cause printed for right-heart failure is ______ heart failure, acting through increased RVEDP.
questions.exp: The top line reads m/c cause: left heart failure, due to increase in RVEDP. (Book p321)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: What pressure sequence leads to the five signs of right-heart failure?
opts: Increased RA pressure → increased venacaval pressures → abdominojugular reflex, ascites, edema, hepatomegaly and raised JVP
Reduced PCWP → diuresis → weight loss, cyanosis and syncope
Reduced JVP → cough, wheeze and hemoptysis
Increased LVEDP → aortic dissection → chest pain and shock
questions.exp: The right-HF flow starts with raised RA and venacaval pressures and ends in those five findings, with AJR called impending RHF. (Book p321)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: At which site is the abdominojugular reflex palpated?
questions.exp: The AJR note reads site of palpation: periumbilical area. (Book p321)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: Match each listed cause of heart failure to its qualifier — 1) Dilated cardiomyopathy 2) Ischemic cardiomyopathy 3) Valvular heart disease 4) Congenital heart disease … A) Severe AR, very severe AS or severe MR B) Genetic cause is most common C) Post-MI/CAD D) No qualifier printed
questions.exp: The causes list genetic as the m/c cause of DCMP, ischemic cardiomyopathy post-MI/CAD, valvular disease with severe AR/very severe AS/severe MR, and congenital disease without qualifier. (Book p321)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: Match the first four major Framingham criteria in printed order — 1) First 2) Second 3) Third 4) Fourth … A) Abdominojugular reflex B) Acute pulmonary edema C) Raised JVP D) Cardiomegaly
questions.exp: The major column begins acute pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, abdominojugular reflex and raised JVP. (Book p321)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: Which final three major Framingham criteria complete the column?
opts: Ankle edema, hepatomegaly and pleural effusion
Nocturnal cough, dyspnea on exertion and tachycardia
questions.exp: Major criteria 5–7 are PND/orthopnea, crepitations/rales and S3 (gallop). (Book p321)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: Match the six minor Framingham criteria in order — 1) First 2) Second 3) Third 4) Fourth 5) Fifth 6) Sixth … A) Pleural effusion B) Ankle edema C) Tachycardia >120 bpm D) Dyspnea on exertion E) Nocturnal cough F) Hepatomegaly
questions.exp: The minor column reads ankle edema, dyspnea on exertion, hepatomegaly, nocturnal cough, pleural effusion and tachycardia >120 bpm. (Book p321)

questions.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the Framingham columns.
opts: False — tachycardia >120 bpm is a major criterion
True — both S3 gallop and ankle edema are major criteria
False — acute pulmonary edema is a minor criterion
True — S3 gallop is a major criterion while ankle edema is a minor criterion
questions.exp: S3 is major item 7, ankle edema minor item 1, tachycardia >120 bpm minor item 6 and acute pulmonary edema major item 1. (Book p321)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: Which chain opens the HFpEF/HFNEF pathophysiology?
opts: Myocardial infarction → papillary muscle rupture → acute MR → shock
Comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation → LV dysfunction → affected longitudinal fibres (untwisting) → LV diastolic dysfunction
Renal-artery stenosis → flash edema → troponin rise → carvedilol
Aortic regurgitation → eccentric hypertrophy → wide pulse pressure → Lincoln sign
questions.exp: The vertical chain begins comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation, LV dysfunction, longitudinal-fibre (untwisting) involvement and LV diastolic dysfunction. (Book p322)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: What happens after LV diastolic dysfunction in the same flowchart?
opts: The aorta regurgitates into the LV, causing wide pulse pressure
The lung develops a pneumatocele, then a thin-walled cavity
The cavity dilates, LVEDP falls and AF risk disappears

Compensatory LVH decreases cavity size, raising LVEDP and LAP; raised PCVP causes interstitial/alveolar edema and dyspnea, while atrial stretch/dilation increases atrial contribution to CO (>40%) and AF risk
questions.exp: The page prints compensation (LVH) → decreased cavity size → ↑LVEDP → ↑LAP, then a PCWP/edema/dyspnea arm and an atrial-stretch arm with >40% atrial CO contribution and AF risk. (Book p322)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: Match each column of the HF-versus-COPD note — 1) Crepitations 2) Peripheries 3) Predominant symptom … A) HF: dyspnea > cough B) HF: fine gravitational crepitations changing with position; COPD: fine crepitations not changing with position C) HF: cold; COPD: warm with CO₂ retention
questions.exp: The three table rows compare positional crepitations, cold versus warm peripheries and dyspnea-dominant HF versus cough-dominant COPD. (Book p322)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: A dyspneic patient has fine gravitational crackles that change with position and cold peripheries. Which side of the printed comparison does this fit?
questions.exp: The HF column pairs position-changing gravitational crepitations with cold peripheries; COPD has non-positional crepitations and warm peripheries. (Book p322)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: How many seconds of bending are specified in the bendopnea note?
questions.exp: The note reads bend for 30 secs → increased venous return → patient symptomatic. (Book p322)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: Match each related term to its printed description — 1) Bendopnea 2) Trepopnea 3) Platypnea … A) Breathlessness lying on one side; right-side preference with right effusion B) Sign of advanced HF made symptomatic by bending C) Printed as a name without a definition on this page
questions.exp: Bendopnea is advanced-HF bending; trepopnea is breathlessness on one side with the right-effusion example; platypnea is only named here. (Book p322)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one line belongs to the HFrEF low-output list, not the p322 HFpEF pathophysiology.
opts: Atrial contribution to cardiac output is >40%
Longitudinal fibres and untwisting are affected
questions.exp: Pulsus alternans is a p319 systolic-failure sign; the other three are in the HFpEF flowchart. (Book p322)

questions.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the p322 HFpEF notes.
opts: False — LVH compensation enlarges the cavity
True — the caption says a right-sided pneumothorax with a shifted mediastinum
True — the chest-film caption says pulmonary edema with pleural effusion on both sides
False — atrial fibrillation risk is reduced by atrial stretch
questions.exp: The image caption reads pulmonary edema with pleural effusion on both sides; atrial stretch increases AF risk and LVH compensation decreases cavity size. (Book p322)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
questions.q: Which three-part definition of HFNEF is attributed to the European Society of Cardiology?
opts: Fever, raised ESR and pericardial enhancement
LV thickness ≥15 mm, small cavity and dynamic LVOT obstruction
Symptoms of congestive heart failure, normal/mildly abnormal LV systolic function and abnormal LV relaxation
Reduced EF <40%, dilated LV and global hypokinesia
questions.exp: The definition bullets are symptoms of CHF, normal/mildly abnormal LV systolic function and abnormal LV relaxation. (Book p323)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
questions.q: How is the presentation of HFNEF described?
opts: Older age groups, more often women, comorbid HTN/obesity/CKD/anemia/diabetes/CAD, and AF more than in HFrEF
Children with Williams syndrome and supravalvular AS
Young athletic males with isolated aortic regurgitation
questions.exp: The presentation bullets list older age, m/c women, the six comorbidities and AF more in HFNEF than HFrEF. (Book p323)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
questions.q: Match each numbered ADHF risk factor to its printed detail — 1) Patient-related 2) Infection 3) Anemia 4) Drug-related … A) NSAIDs; naproxen printed as safest in HF B) Non-compliance to treatment C) CAD on aspirin → GI bleed → anemia → decompensation D) LRTI/IE
questions.exp: The risk list gives non-compliance, LRTI/IE, the aspirin–GI-bleed–anemia chain, and NSAIDs/CCBs under drug-related decompensation. (Book p323)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
questions.q: Which CCBs and rhythm are emphasised in the ADHF risk list?
opts: Amlodipine/nifedipine improve LV function; sinus bradycardia is most important
Verapamil prevents GI bleeding; AF is protective
Verapamil/diltiazem depress LV function; atrial fibrillation is the most important arrhythmia
Diltiazem is the safest NSAID; VT is most important
questions.exp: The drug bullet names verapamil/diltiazem as depressing LV function, and the arrhythmia bullet names AF as most important. (Book p323)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
questions.q: Which NSAID does the page print as the safest in heart failure?
questions.exp: The NSAID sub-bullet reads 'Safest NSAID in HF → Naproxen' as a source note, not a prescribing instruction. (Book p323)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation

opts: Aortic dissection, trauma, sinus of Valsalva rupture and IE
Renal failure, pregnancy, uncontrolled hypertension and myocardial ischemia
questions.exp: Items 5–8 are renal failure, pregnancy, uncontrolled HTN and myocardial ischemia. (Book p323)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation

opts: Valve stenosis → gradient → AVR → prosthesis → anticoagulation
Infection → myocarditis → Dallas criteria → steroids → LV rupture
Index event (DCM, ischemia) → HFrEF → compensatory mechanisms → cardiac remodelling → maintain CO
questions.exp: The line reads index event (DCM, ischemia) → HFrEF → compensatory mechanisms → cardiac remodelling → maintain CO. (Book p323)

questions.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
questions.q: The first compensatory mechanism is increased sympathetic activity, which increases contractility and heart rate and makes the patient prone to ______.
questions.exp: The sympathetic branch reads increased activity → increased contractility/HR → prone for arrhythmias. (Book p323)

questions.sec: RAAS, ADH and Natriuretic-Peptide Compensation, the Treatment Logic and the Initial Beta-Blocker and ACE/ARB Choices
questions.q: Match each compensatory mechanism to its printed effect — 1) Angiotensin II 2) Aldosterone 3) ADH 4) Natriuretic peptides … A) Salt and water retention → raised preload B) Vasoconstriction → raised afterload C) Inhibit RAAS/sympathetic and excrete salt and water D) Free-water retention → hyponatremia
questions.exp: The p324 bullets map angiotensin II to afterload, aldosterone to preload, ADH to free-water retention/hyponatremia and natriuretic peptides to inhibition/excretion. (Book p324)

questions.sec: RAAS, ADH and Natriuretic-Peptide Compensation, the Treatment Logic and the Initial Beta-Blocker and ACE/ARB Choices

They close the aortic valve and abolish regurgitation
They produce polycythemia and pulmonary hypertension
Secondary end-organ damage within the ventricle worsens LV remodelling and leads to subsequent cardiac decompensation
questions.exp: The note reads sustained activation of compensatory mechanisms (1, 2, 3) → secondary end-organ damage within ventricle → worsens LV remodelling → subsequent cardiac decompensation. (Book p324)

questions.sec: RAAS, ADH and Natriuretic-Peptide Compensation, the Treatment Logic and the Initial Beta-Blocker and ACE/ARB Choices

The coronary pathway, platelet adhesion and fibrinolysis
The pulmonary pathway, surfactant and ciliary clearance
The vagal pathway, coagulation and vitamin D absorption

questions.exp: The ADH bullet reads free water retention → hyponatremia. (Book p324)

units.title: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
units.sec: The ACC/AHA 2017 Definition, the Four Heart-Failure Types and the Complete NYHA Classification Table
units.guide:
The ACC/AHA 2017 definition calls heart failure a complex clinical syndrome from structural/functional cardiac disease that impairs ventricular filling or ejection; structural LVH and functional AF are the examples, and the printed ACC/AHA expansions are retained (p318).
The four types are HFrEF EF <40%, HFpEF/HFNEF EF ≥50%, HFmrEF EF 40–50% and ADHF. The NYHA first-line symptoms are angina, dyspnea and palpitation; syncope is explicitly excluded.
NYHA I–IV progress from symptoms with more than ordinary activity, ordinary activity, less than ordinary activity to rest; the mortality column gives negligible mortality, sudden cardiac death across II–III and LV-failure symptoms in IV.

units.title: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
units.sec: The A-to-D Stages, the Most Common Presentation, and the Ten Low-Output Systolic-Failure Features
units.guide:
Stage A has risk factors (HTN, atherosclerosis, DM, OSA) without symptoms or structural disease; stage B has structural disease without symptoms (HTN → LVH, previous MI → remodelling); stage C is the commonest and symptomatic; stage D is refractory to medical therapy (p319).
The most common overall presentation is HFrEF, NYHA 2/3, stage C.
Systolic LV-forward failure from reduced cardiac output lists fatigue with cachexia/TNF-α, decreased urine output, cool extremities, cyanosis, altered mentation, S3, cardiomegaly/dilated LV, displaced apex, pulsus alternans and narrow pulse pressure.

units.title: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
units.sec: The Diastolic-Failure Pressure Chain, Dyspnea, Crackles and Effusion, and the Orthopnea and PND Mechanisms
units.guide:
Concentric LVH reducing cavity size and systolic failure with insufficient dilation/increased ESV both raise LVEDP; the chain continues through LAP and PCVP to pulmonary exudation (p320).
Its consequences are dyspnea (predominant symptom), acute crackles and predominantly right-sided pleural effusion with right-side lying preference. Orthopnea is immediate on lying down; PND occurs after 2–3 hours.
PND follows supine posture → increased interstitial-to-intravascular fluid shift → RA → pulmonary circulation → failure to accommodate the load → air hunger.

units.title: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
units.sec: Right-Heart Failure, the Abdominojugular Reflex, the Four Causes and the Framingham Major and Minor Criteria
units.guide:
Right-heart failure is most often caused by left-heart failure through raised RVEDP, then raised RA and venacaval pressures produce impending AJR, ascites, edema, hepatomegaly and raised JVP; AJR is palpated periumbilically (p321).
Causes are DCMP (genetic cause most common), ischemic cardiomyopathy post-MI/CAD, valvular disease (severe AR, very severe AS or severe MR) and congenital heart disease.
Framingham major criteria are acute pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, AJR, raised JVP, PND/orthopnea, crepitations/rales and S3 gallop; minor criteria are ankle edema, exertional dyspnea, hepatomegaly, nocturnal cough, pleural effusion and tachycardia >120 bpm.

units.title: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
units.sec: HFpEF/HFNEF Pathophysiology, the Heart-Failure-versus-COPD Table and Bendopnea, Trepopnea and Platypnea
units.guide:
HFpEF/HFNEF begins with comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation → LV dysfunction → longitudinal-fibre/untwisting dysfunction → LV diastolic dysfunction (p322). Compensatory LVH reduces cavity size and raises LVEDP and LAP.
One arm raises PCWP to produce interstitial/alveolar edema and dyspnea; the other stretches/dilates the atria, raises their CO contribution >40% and predisposes to AF. The film caption shows bilateral pulmonary edema and pleural effusions.
HF has position-changing gravitational crepitations, cold peripheries and dyspnea > cough; COPD has non-positional fine crepitations, warm CO₂-retaining peripheries and cough > dyspnea. Bendopnea is advanced HF with 30 seconds of bending; trepopnea is breathlessness on one side (right-side preference with right effusion); platypnea is named without definition.

units.title: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
units.sec: The European HFNEF Definition and Presentation, Ten Decompensation Risk Factors, Pathogenesis and Sympathetic Activation
units.guide:
The ESC HFNEF definition needs CHF symptoms, normal/mildly abnormal LV systolic function and abnormal LV relaxation; typical patients are older women with HTN, obesity, CKD, anemia, diabetes or CAD and more AF than HFrEF (p323).
ADHF risk factors are non-compliance, LRTI/IE, anemia from CAD aspirin → GI bleed, renal failure, pregnancy, uncontrolled HTN, myocardial ischemia, NSAIDs (naproxen printed as safest in HF), LV-depressing verapamil/diltiazem, and arrhythmias—especially AF.
HFrEF pathogenesis runs index event (DCM/ischemia) → HFrEF → compensation → remodelling to maintain CO; sympathetic activation raises contractility and HR but predisposes to arrhythmias.

units.title: RAAS, ADH and Natriuretic-Peptide Compensation, the Treatment Logic and the Initial Beta-Blocker and ACE/ARB Choices
units.sec: RAAS, ADH and Natriuretic-Peptide Compensation, the Treatment Logic and the Initial Beta-Blocker and ACE/ARB Choices
units.guide:
RAAS compensation raises afterload through angiotensin II and preload through aldosterone-mediated salt/water retention; ADH retains free water and causes hyponatremia, while natriuretic peptides inhibit RAAS/sympathetic activity and excrete salt and water (p324).
Sustained activation of mechanisms 1–3 causes secondary end-organ damage, worsens LV remodelling and leads to decompensation. Nesiritide is printed as no longer used; treatment blocks sympathetic activity, RAAS and degradation of natriuretic peptides with a neprilysin inhibitor.
Beta blockers include metoprolol, bisoprolol (most preferred, 1.25 mg) and carvedilol (3.125 mg BD). ACE inhibitors/ARBs have a class effect, with ramipril/perindopril named and ACE > ARB because ACE raises bradykinin.

units.title: ARNI, the Treatment Hierarchy, Euvolemia and Renal-Failure Caveats, the Fantastic Four and Refractory Heart Failure
units.sec: ARNI, the Treatment Hierarchy, Euvolemia and Renal-Failure Caveats, the Fantastic Four and Refractory Heart Failure
units.guide:
ARNI combines valsartan (ARB) and sacubitril (NI), with the printed diagram wording preserved as a source caveat (p325). Natriuretic peptides listed are ANP, BNP, substance P, adrenomedulline and bradykinin.
Primary management for all HF is ARNI + beta blocker, ranked ARNI > beta blocker > ACE inhibitor > ARB; if the patient is not euvolemic, diuretics must come first to avoid pulmonary edema. Renal-failure HF is paired with hydralazine + nitrate.
The Fantastic Four are ARNI, beta blocker, non-steroidal aldosterone antagonist finerenone and SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin/dapagliflozin). If refractory and HR >70/min, ivabradine (funny-current inhibitor; visual disturbances) is added; wide-QRS refractory HF goes to CRT then transplant, while normal QRS goes to LV assist devices or ICD.
